elements.name: Traceability
elements.documentation: The ability to track a product’s journey from origin to end-user – is crucial for non-profit and Public Health work. Whether distributing medicines, food aid, or other essential goods, organizations need end-to-end visibility to ensure products are authentic, safely handled, and actually reach intended beneficiaries. By assigning unique identifiers to products and capturing their movements in a digital system, stakeholders can quickly pinpoint where an item is at any given time or isolate issues (like a bad batch of medication) and initiate targeted recalls[1]. In low-resource settings, improving traceability boosts trust and reduces fraud, theft, and counterfeiting – common problems that undermine humanitarian efforts[2][3]. Overall, robust traceability systems enhance transparency and accountability, which are core values in Public Health supply chains.

elements.name: Interoperability & Health Information Exchange
elements.documentation:
This capability provides the technical infrastructure and standards required for different health IT systems to talk to each other and share data. It involves the use of common APIs, messaging standards, and exchange protocols.

The purpose is to enable a unified patient view by connecting fragmented health data sources across the entire health system. This is the primary driver for clinical coordination and longitudinal record creation.
Example: A national HIE hub that routes clinical 
summaries between public clinics and private specialist centers.

elements.name: Data Sharing & Authorization
elements.documentation:
This capability handles the technical processes of exchanging data between systems based on authorized requests and valid consent. It ensures that data flows securely and only to parties who have the legal right to see it.

The purpose is to enable seamless interoperability while strictly enforcing access control policies. This allows for clinical data to follow the patient across different levels of care without compromising privacy.

Example: An authorization server issuing temporary tokens to allow a lab system to push results to a patient’s PHR.

elements.name: Universal Access Enablement
elements.documentation:
This capability ensures that personal health services and records are accessible to all citizens through multiple channels, including web portals and mobile devices. It focuses on inclusivity and reducing barriers to health information access.

The purpose is to drive widespread adoption and ensure that all individuals, regardless of their location or device, can benefit from their health data. This supports the goal of equitable access to modern health services.

Example: A multi-channel PHR portal that works on both high-end smartphones and basic feature phones via USSD.

elements.documentation:

The purpose is to achieve semantic interoperability, where systems can accurately interpret and act upon the data they receive. This is essential for clinical decision support, analytics, and reporting.

Example: A central terminology server that maps local hospital "chest pain" codes to the international ICD-11 standard.

Example: Implementing end-to-end encryption for all patient data stored in the national PHR repository.

elements.name: Product
elements.documentation:
The concrete offering, which is made available to stakeholders. 

It bundles together services, data, and rules into a package that delivers value. Products make capabilities consumable by users. 

For example, the Trusted Personal Health Record or the National Surveillance Dashboard are products delivered in the DPI-H context.



A product represents a coherent collection of services and/or passive structure elements, accompanied by a contract, which is offered as a whole to (internal or external) customers. 



This definition covers both intangible, services-based, or information products that are common in information-intensive organizations, as well as tangible, physical products. A financial or information product consists of a collection of services along with a contract that specifies the characteristics, rights, and requirements associated with the product. “Buying” a product gives the customer the right to use the associated services. Generally, the product element is used to specify a product type. The number of product types in an organization is typically relatively stable compared to the processes that realize or support the products. “Buying” is usually one of the services associated with a product which results in a new instance of that product (belonging to a specific customer). Similarly, there may be services to modify or destroy a product. A product may aggregate or compose business services, application services, technology services, business objects, data objects, and technology passive structure elements (artifacts and material), as well as a contract. Hence a product may aggregate or compose elements from other layers than the Business Layer. A value may be associated with a product. The name of a product is usually the name used in the communication with customers, or possibly a more generic noun (e.g., “travel insurance”).

elements.name: Application Service (MS)
elements.documentation:
An explicitly defined application behavior. An application service exposes the functionality of components to their environment. 


It is the IT functionality that fulfills the business outcome. Application services are expressed as useful units of behavior. They link business capabilities to the application that enables them.

For example, “Consent Management Service” or “FHIR API Service”. 

This functionality is accessed through one or more application interfaces and is realized by one or more application functions that are performed by the component. It may require, use, and produce data objects. An application service should be meaningful from the point of view of the environment; it should provide a unit of behavior that is, in itself, useful to its users. It has a purpose that states this utility to the environment in terms of the value it delivers, modeled as a value element associated with the service. This means that if this environment includes business processes, application services should have business relevance. An application service may serve business, application, and technology behavior or active structure elements. An application function or process may realize an application service. An application interface may be assigned to an application service. An application service may access data objects. The name of an application service should preferably be a verb ending with “-ing”; e.g., “transaction processing”. Also, a name explicitly containing the word “service” may be used.

elements.name: Consent Management Platform
elements.documentation:
The Consent Management Platform is a technical component that manages the capture, storage, and enforcement of patient preferences regarding the sharing of their health information. It provides a mechanism for patients to grant, modify, or revoke access to specific data segments or healthcare providers.

Its purpose is to operationalize patient agency by ensuring that health data is only shared according to the individual's explicit authorization. It provides a transparent mechanism for patients to govern their own health data privacy and builds trust in digital systems.

Example: A digital dashboard where a patient can grant a specific cardiologist temporary access to their diagnostic imaging results.

elements.name: IAM/Access Control System
elements.documentation:
The IAM/Access Control System handles the authentication and authorization of all users and systems in the health network. It utilizes identity federation and token-based mechanisms to grant appropriate access rights based on specific user roles and permissions.

Its purpose is to ensure that only authorized personnel can access sensitive patient information according to established security and privacy policies. It protects the system from unauthorized entry while providing a seamless login experience for legitimate users.

Example: A system that uses multi-factor authentication to verify a physician's identity before allowing them to access or edit a clinical care plan.

elements.name: Terminology Service (SNOMED, ICD, LOINC)
elements.documentation:
This service provides a centralized source for standardized clinical codes and vocabularies. It supports the translation and mapping between different medical coding systems.

The purpose is to ensure that clinical data retains its meaning as it moves between different healthcare systems. This is the technical enabler for semantic interoperability and meaningful analytics.

Example: A service that tells a reporting system that the local code "C-19" should be mapped to the ICD-10 code "U07.1".

elements.name: Authorization & Access Control Service
elements.documentation:
This service is a technical component that manages and enforces the rules and permissions for accessing health data within the TPHR ecosystem. it works in conjunction with identity services to ensure that only verified users with the correct privileges can interact with sensitive medical records.

The purpose is to provide robust security and privacy by validating that every data request aligns with the patient’s explicit consent and the provider’s specific clinical role. This prevents the unauthorized exposure of personal information and ensures the integrity of the information exchange network.

Example: A service that grants a physician "read-only" access to a patient's surgical history while automatically blocking access to their confidential counseling notes.

elements.name: Encryption & Key Management Service
elements.documentation:
This service manages the cryptographic keys used for data encryption and decryption across the ecosystem. It ensures that the keys are stored securely and only accessible to authorized processes.

The purpose is to provide the underlying security mechanism for protecting data privacy. Effective key management is essential for the long-term safety of encrypted health information.

Example: A service that rotates the database encryption keys every 90 days to maintain high security standards.

elements.name: Record Verification Service
elements.documentation:
This service handles the management of digital certificates, keys, and the verification of cryptographic signatures. It provides the technical proof required for trust in digital transactions.

The purpose is to ensure that any document or exchange in the system is authentic and has not been tampered with. This supports non-repudiation and legal validity of digital health records.

Example: A service that verifies the digital signature on a lab result before it is automatically added to a patient’s PHR.

elements.name: Client Registry
elements.documentation:
The Client Registry is a master patient index and identity provider that manages demographic details and unique identifiers for health system users. It maintains relationships among records to handle merged or linked identities across different health programs and facilities.

Its purpose is to provide a unique, verifiable patient identity that links medical records across disparate and fragmented sources. It ensures accurate patient identification, which is critical for patient safety and the creation of longitudinal health records.

Example: A central system that maps a citizen's national ID to their specific medical record IDs in multiple regional hospitals.

elements.name: Audit & Compliance Engine
elements.documentation:
The Audit & Compliance Engine is a component that records and monitors all activities and transactions within the health information network for security and regulatory compliance. It generates non-repudiable logs of who accessed which data and when to ensure full accountability across the ecosystem.

Its purpose is to ensure the security and integrity of health data by providing a traceable record of system usage and data access events. It supports governance by identifying potential breaches or unauthorized access through continuous oversight of the technical environment.

Example: A backend service that logs every instance of a clinician viewing a patient's sensitive medical history or personal data.

elements.name: Interoperability Middleware
elements.documentation:
Interoperability Middleware is a software layer that facilitates the secure exchange of health information between disparate systems using standardized protocols like FHIR or IHE. Its purpose is to bridge technical gaps between legacy and modern health IT systems, enabling a unified data flow across the healthcare ecosystem. It ensures that clinical data can be shared across institutional boundaries without requiring a single monolithic system.

elements.name: Application Service
elements.documentation:
An explicitly defined application behavior. An application service exposes the functionality of components to their environment. 


It is the IT functionality that fulfills the business outcome. Application services are expressed as useful units of behavior. They link business capabilities to the application that enables them.

For example, “Consent Management Service” or “FHIR API Service”. 

This functionality is accessed through one or more application interfaces and is realized by one or more application functions that are performed by the component. It may require, use, and produce data objects. An application service should be meaningful from the point of view of the environment; it should provide a unit of behavior that is, in itself, useful to its users. It has a purpose that states this utility to the environment in terms of the value it delivers, modeled as a value element associated with the service. This means that if this environment includes business processes, application services should have business relevance. An application service may serve business, application, and technology behavior or active structure elements. An application function or process may realize an application service. An application interface may be assigned to an application service. An application service may access data objects. The name of an application service should preferably be a verb ending with “-ing”; e.g., “transaction processing”. Also, a name explicitly containing the word “service” may be used.

elements.name: Establish a secure, universally accessible, verifiable health record for every individual
elements.documentation:
This sub-goal aims to create a national infrastructure where every citizen has a digital health record that is secure and universally available. It focuses on issuing verifiable credentials that can be used across the entire care continuum.

The purpose is to ensure life-long health data portability and continuity of care for all individuals. It addresses the "Right to Health" by providing an equitable and person-centric data ownership model.

Example: A national mandate to issue a digital health identity and record to every newborn and existing citizen.

elements.name: Enable patient control and consent-based sharing of health information
elements.documentation:
This subgoal focuses on empowering individuals to manage access to their health data through granular, explicit consent mechanisms. It transitions the health ecosystem toward a model where patients govern who sees their information and for what purpose.

The objective is to ensure ethical data use and comply with legal requirements for informed consent. It builds systemic trust by providing patients with agency and digital empowerment over their personal health journey.

A citizen using a digital dashboard to grant a specialist temporary access to their specific lab results for a consultation.

elements.name: Develop a secure and universally accessible system for issuing verifiable digital health records to individuals for their utilization as they seek care, following appropriate safeguards for privacy, security and consent
elements.documentation:
This goal involves establishing a secure and universally accessible infrastructure for issuing verifiable digital health records to all individuals. It creates a standardized system where personal medical data is portable and remains under the individual's control as they move through the healthcare system.

The purpose is to foster patient empowerment and ensure seamless continuity of care by providing trusted data at the point of service. It aims to reduce clinical errors and administrative fragmentation through a robust framework for privacy, security, and informed consent.

Example: A national digital health app that allows citizens to receive, store, and present verifiable medical certificates and lab results during consultations.

elements.name: Support interoperability across providers, facilities, and jurisdictions
elements.documentation:
This subgoal focuses on eliminating data silos by adopting standardized protocols and clinical terminologies for seamless information exchange. It enables health data to flow accurately and meaningfully between different facilities and geographic regions.

The purpose is to reduce record fragmentation and improve care coordination by ensuring patient data is machine-readable by any authorized system. It supports global mobility and effective public health monitoring through the use of standardized data formats.

Requiring all public and private hospitals to use the HL7 FHIR standard for sharing clinical summaries.

elements.name: Population has verifiable digital health records
elements.documentation:
This outcome is achieved when the majority of citizens are issued secure, digital health credentials that are recognized across the country. It signifies the transition from paper-based or fragmented records to a trusted national digital infrastructure.

The purpose is to provide a foundation for modern, data-driven healthcare that is person-centric and portable. It enables the systemic benefits of improved data quality, better care coordination, and citizen empowerment.

Example: 90% of the population possessing a digital health record that is recognized by all public and private providers.

elements.name: Goal
elements.documentation:
A high-level statement of intent, direction, or desired state for an organization and its stakeholders. 

Goals are expressed qualitatively, and can represent anything a stakeholder may desire, such as a state of affairs, or a produced value.  Goals define direction and intention, and may be broken into smaller sub-goals or linked to measurable outcomes. 

Goals are typically used to measure success of an organization and it is common to associate concrete outcomes with goals. 



Examples:

* Universal access to personal health records

* Optimize Supply Chain Management

* Enhance Climate Resilience with Predictive Capabilities

elements.name: Outcome
elements.documentation:
An end result, effect, or consequence of a certain state of affairs. 

A Business Outcome is what is actually achieved by implementing capabilities—it is the tangible, often measurable result. Outcomes are frequently tied to KPIs and may be time-bound. Outcomes can also be used to model potentially unwanted effects; for example, in order to design appropriate mitigating measures.

For example, “80% of citizens issued with a verifiable health record” or “90% of adverse events reported within 24 hours”. Outcomes demonstrate whether the architecture is delivering on its goals.

For example, a citizen values secure access to their data, while a health worker values having a complete clinical history at the point of care.
